plain_english:
When I look at myself honestly, Seneca, some of my faults are right there on the surface where I can grab hold of them. Others are harder to see and harder to reach. And some come and go — they disappear for a while, then return when I least expect them. These last ones are the worst. They're like an enemy who attacks whenever you let your guard down. You can't prepare for them like you would in a war, but you can't relax either, the way you would in peacetime.

The state I find myself in most often — and why shouldn't I tell you the truth, the way I would with a doctor? — is this: I'm not completely free of the faults I fear and hate, but I'm not entirely controlled by them either. My condition isn't the worst it could be, but it's restless and irritable. I'm neither sick nor well.

It's no use telling me that all virtues start out weak and grow stronger with time. I already know that. Even the superficial ones — an impressive reputation, a talent for speaking, anything that impresses other people — gain power over the years. The virtues that give us real inner strength and the ones that just make us look good both take a long time to settle in. But what I'm afraid of is this: the same force of habit that strengthens good qualities may also be driving my faults deeper into me. Spend enough time around both good and bad people, and you start treating them all the same.

What this weakness really looks like — when your mind hovers between two sides without leaning strongly toward good or evil — I can show you better in pieces than all at once.
original_excerpt:
When I examine myself, Seneca, some vices appear on the surface,
and so that I can lay my hands upon them, while others are less
distinct and harder to reach, and some are not always present, but
recur at intervals: and these I should call the most troublesome,
being like a roving enemy that assails one when he sees his
opportunity, and who will neither let one stand on one's guard as
in war, nor yet take one's rest without fear as in peace. The
position in which I find myself more especially (for why should I
not tell you the truth as I would to a physician), is that of neither
being thoroughly set free from the vices which I fear and hate, nor
yet quite in bondage to them: my state of mind, though not the worst
possible, is a particularly discontented and sulky one: I am neither
ill nor well, It is of no use for you to tell me that all virtues
are weakly at the outset, and that they acquire strength and solidity
by time, for I am well aware that even those which do but help our
outward show, such as grandeur, a reputation for eloquence, and
everything that appeals to others, gain power by time. Both those
which afford us real strength and those which do but trick
us out in a more attractive form, require long years before they
gradually are adapted to us by time. But I fear that custom, which
confirms most things, implants this vice more and more deeply in
me. Long acquaintance with both good and bad people leads one to
esteem them all alike. What this state of weakness really is, when
the mind halts between two opinions without any strong inclination
towards either good or evil, I shall be better able to show you
piecemeal than all at once.

plain_english:
Let me tell you what happens to me — you can diagnose the condition. I have to admit: I truly love living simply. I don't want a bed draped in fancy fabrics, or clothes pulled from a trunk, pressed flat under weights, and polished with endless ironing. Give me something plain and cheap that takes no effort to store or put on. For food, I don't want dishes that need a small army to prepare and present, or meals ordered days ahead and carried in by a parade of hands. I want something easy and ready to eat, nothing exotic or expensive — available anywhere, a burden to neither my wallet nor my body, and unlikely to come back up the way it went down. I like a rough, unpolished servant raised at home. I like the heavy silver plate my country-born father owned, stamped with no famous maker's name. I don't want a table admired for its beautiful patterns, or known all over town because of the string of fashionable owners who've had it before me — just one that serves its purpose and doesn't make any guest stare with longing or burn with envy.

But even while I'm perfectly content with all this, something catches me off guard. I notice the clothes of some rich man's schoolboy, dressed with uncommon care and elegance. I see slaves decked in gold and a whole gleaming regiment of attendants. I think of houses where you walk on precious stones, where valuables are scattered in every corner, where even the ceilings are brilliantly painted — and a whole household escorts an inheritance down the road to ruin. And what about those banquets? Crystal-clear water flowing around the guests, feasts staged like theatre productions. Coming from my long stretch of plain living, I suddenly find myself surrounded by dazzling luxury on every side. My eyes start to waver. I can hold my heart steady against it more easily than my gaze.

When I come home from seeing all this, I'm sadder — though not worse. I can't walk among my own humble things with quite the same confidence as before. A quiet irritation creeps in, and a doubt: maybe that way of living is better than mine. None of it changes my principles. But all of it unsettles me.
original_excerpt:
I will tell you what befalls me, you
must find out the name of the disease. I have to confess the greatest
possible love of thrift: I do not care for a bed with gorgeous
hangings, nor for clothes brought out of a chest, or pressed under
weights and made glossy by frequent manglings, but for common and
cheap ones, that require no care either to keep them or to put them
on. For food I do not want what needs whole troops of servants to
prepare it and admire it, nor what is ordered many days before and
served up by many hands, but something handy and easily come at,
with nothing far-fetched or costly about it, to be had in every
part of the world, burdensome neither to one's fortune nor one's
body, not likely to go out of the body by the same path by which
it came in. I like[1] a rough and unpolished homebred servant, I
like my servant born in my house: I like my country-bred father's
heavy silver plate stamped with no maker's name: I do not want a
table that is beauteous with dappled spots, or known to all the
town by the number of fashionable people to whom it has successively
belonged, but one which stands merely for use, and which causes no
guest's eye to dwell upon it with pleasure or to kindle at it with
envy. While I am well satisfied with this, I am reminded of the
clothes of a certain schoolboy, dressed with no ordinary care and
splendour, of slaves bedecked with gold and a whole regiment
of glittering attendants. I think of houses too, where one treads
on precious stones, and where valuables lie about in every corner,
where the very roof is brilliantly painted, and a whole nation
attends and accompanies an inheritance on the road to ruin. What
shall I say of waters, transparent to the very bottom, which flow
round the guests, and banquets worthy of the theatre in which they
take place? Coming as I do from a long course of dull thrift, I
find myself surrounded by the most brilliant luxury, which echoes
around me on every side: my sight becomes a little dazzled by it:
I can lift up my heart against it more easily than my eyes. When I
return from seeing it I am a sadder, though not a worse man, I
cannot walk amid my own paltry possessions with so lofty a step as
before, and silently there steals over me a feeling of vexation,
and a doubt whether that way of life may not be better than mine.
None of these things alter my principles, yet all of them disturb me.

plain_english: Sometimes I follow the teachings of our school and throw myself into public life. I chase office and aim for the highest ranks — not because I'm drawn to the robes and symbols of power, but so I can help my friends, my family, my fellow citizens, and really everyone. Full of purpose, I follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, all of whom told us to take part in public affairs — even though none of them ever did so themselves. But then, the moment something rattles my mind — which isn't built for shocks — or something embarrassing happens (as it does in every life), or things don't go smoothly, or some trivial matter eats up far too much of my time, I retreat back into leisure. Like tired cattle that pick up speed when they're heading home, I want to withdraw and live quietly within my own walls. "No one," I tell myself, "is going to steal a single day from me without giving me something worth the loss. Let my mind stay with itself and grow. Let it have nothing to do with other people's business, nothing that depends on anyone else's approval. Let me enjoy a peace undisturbed by public or private troubles."
original_excerpt:
At one time I would obey the maxims of our school and plunge
into public life, I would obtain office and become consul, not
because the purple robe and lictor's axes attract me, but in order
that I may be able to be of use to my friends, my relatives, to all
my countrymen, and indeed to all mankind. Ready and determined, I
follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, all of whom
bid one take part in public affairs, though none of them ever did
so himself: and then, as soon as something disturbs my mind, which
is not used to receiving shocks, as soon as something occurs which
is either disgraceful, such as often occurs in all men's lives, or
which does not proceed quite easily, or when subjects of very little
importance require me to devote a great deal of time to them, I go
back to my life of leisure, and, just as even tired cattle go faster
when they are going home, I wish to retire and pass my life within
the walls of my house. "No one," I say, "that will give me no
compensation worth such a loss shall ever rob me of a day.
Let my mind be contained within itself and improve itself: let it
take no part with other men's affairs, and do nothing which depends
on the approval of others: let me enjoy a tranquillity undisturbed
by either public or private troubles."

plain_english:
But whenever I read something courageous and it fires me up, or a noble example pushes me to act, I want to rush into the courts — to lend my voice to one person, my help to another, to try to be useful even if I might fail, or to cut down some lawyer swollen with undeserved success. But then I think — by Hercules — that in philosophy it's better to see things as they are, to speak about them plainly, and to let your words follow the subject rather than dressing them up. "Why build something meant to last forever? Don't you only want that so future generations will talk about you? Yet you were born to die, and a quiet death is the least miserable kind. So write simply, just to pass the time, for yourself, not for an audience. You don't need to work so hard when you're not trying to impress anyone beyond the present moment."

But then again, when my mind is lifted by grand thoughts, it starts reaching for grand words too. The higher the idea, the more elevated the language it demands, and my speech rises to match the subject. In those moments I forget my calm, moderate intentions and soar higher than usual, using a voice that isn't really mine.

I won't pile on more examples. In everything I do, this weakness of a well-meaning mind follows me. I'm afraid I'm slowly sinking to its level — or worse, that I'll always hang there on the edge of falling, with more wrong with me than I realize. We judge our own lives too kindly, and bias always clouds our sight.

I believe many people would have reached wisdom if they hadn't already convinced themselves they'd arrived — if they hadn't deliberately lied to themselves about some flaws and walked right past others with their eyes shut. You have no reason to think that other people's flattery does more damage than your own. Who dares to tell himself the truth? Who — no matter how large a crowd of fawning admirers surrounds him — isn't still his own greatest flatterer?

I beg you, then, if you have any cure that could stop this back-and-forth in me, consider me worthy of owing my peace of mind to you. I know these swings aren't dangerous. They don't threaten any serious breakdown. To put it in an exact comparison: I'm not caught in a storm — I'm just seasick. Take this trouble from me, whatever it is, and help someone who is struggling within sight of land.
original_excerpt:
But whenever my spirit is
roused by reading some brave words, or some noble example spurs me
into action, I want to rush into the law courts, to place my voice
at one man's disposal, my services at another's, and to try to help
him even though I may not succeed, or to quell the pride of some
lawyer who is puffed up by ill-deserved success: but I think, by
Hercules, that in philosophical speculation it is better to view
things as they are, and to speak of them on their own account, and
as for words, to trust to things for them, and to let one's speech
simply follow whither they lead. "Why do you want to construct a
fabric that will endure for ages? Do you not wish to do this in
order that posterity may talk of you: yet you were born to die, and
a silent death is the least wretched. Write something therefore in
a simple style, merely to pass the time, for your own use, and not
for publication. Less labour is needed when one does not look beyond
the present." Then again, when the mind is elevated by the greatness
of its thoughts, it becomes ostentatious in its use of words, the
loftier its aspirations, the more loftily it desires to express
them, and its speech rises to the dignity of its subject. At such
times I forget my mild and moderate determination and soar higher
than is my wont, using a language that is not my own. Not to multiply
examples, I am in all things attended by this weakness of a
well-meaning mind, to whose level I fear that I shall be gradually
brought down, or, what is even more worrying, that I may always
hang as though about to fall, and that there may be more the matter
with me than I myself perceive: for we take a friendly view of our
own private affairs, and partiality always obscures our judgment.
I fancy that many men would have arrived at wisdom had they
not believed themselves to have arrived there already, had they not
purposely deceived themselves as to some parts of their character,
and passed by others with their eyes shut: for you have no grounds
for supposing that other people's flattery is more ruinous to us
than our own. Who dares to tell himself the truth? Who is there,
by however large a troop of caressing courtiers he may be surrounded,
who in spite of them is not his own greatest flatterer? I beg you,
therefore, if you have any remedy by which you could stop this
vacillation of mine, to deem me worthy to owe my peace of mind to
you. I am well aware that these oscillations of mind are not perilous
and that they threaten me with no serious disorder: to express what
I complain of by an exact simile, I am not suffering from a storm,
but from sea-sickness. Take from me, then, this evil, whatever it
may be, and help one who is in distress within sight of land.
